opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a big moment for me, but maybe not in the way people would expect. That was the Holistically-Nested Edge Detection work, HED, which I did with Zhuowen Tu when I was still quite early in my PhD at UCSD. At that time I didn't really have a clear picture of myself as a "researcher." I was just a student trying things, hoping something would work.

When we got the Marr Prize honorable mention, the first feeling was surprise, almost disbelief. ICCV is a place where you see all the people whose papers you've been reading, and suddenly your name is up there with them. So the most immediate effect was confidence. It told me that maybe my instincts were not totally wrong, that the way I thought about problems could actually produce something the community cared about.

But I think the more lasting lesson was about what kind of research matters. Edge detection is a very old, very classical problem. Many people thought it was kind of "solved," or at least not exciting anymore. What made HED work was bringing the deep learning mindset, end-to-end training, deep supervision, multi-scale side outputs, to a problem that people used to attack with hand-crafted features. So it taught me that you don't always need to chase the newest problem. Sometimes revisiting a fundamental problem with a new lens is where the real progress comes from. That idea has stayed with me through ResNeXt, through later work on representation learning, even now.

At the same time, I tried not to let it define me too much. Awards are nice, but they are a bit of a lagging signal; they tell you something you did in the past was good. The danger is you start optimizing for recognition instead of for curiosity. So I'd say it gave me permission to believe I could do this long term, and it also made me a bit more careful: the goal is to keep asking good questions, not to repeat the thing that got you the prize.

r001.rationale: He says the recognition gave him confidence and permission to believe he could do research long term, but describes himself at the time as lacking a clear picture of himself as a researcher. He does not characterize it as the beginning of his life as a researcher.

r002.rationale: He does not say the recognition led him to expect more frequent Best Paper awards. He instead calls awards a lagging signal and cautions against optimizing for recognition.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't really know how to process it. That was 2015, the HED paper, holistically-nested edge detection, and I was still a PhD student at UCSD working with Zhuowen Tu. Edge detection was this very old, very classical problem in computer vision. People had been working on it for decades, Canny and all of that. So when we brought deep learning into it and it worked well, I think part of me just assumed it was a nice result on a niche problem, and that was it.

So the honorable mention was a surprise. I remember being in the ICCV session in Santiago and not quite believing it when they read the title. What it did for me, more than anything, was give me a kind of permission. Before that, I had this quiet doubt, which I think a lot of students have, about whether I actually belonged in this field or whether I was just following along behind the people who were really driving things. Getting that recognition from the community, on a paper where the ideas were largely mine and Zhuowen's, made me feel like, okay, maybe I can have my own taste. Maybe I can pick problems that I find interesting, even if they seem old or unfashionable, and trust that if the work is good, people will notice.

The other thing it did was shape how I think about what makes a paper matter. HED wasn't the biggest model or the flashiest result. The idea was really about multi-scale supervision, about forcing the network to produce meaningful outputs at every level, not just the end. That's a simple idea. And I learned that simple, clean ideas that change how you think about a problem tend to have a longer life than complicated ones. That lesson stayed with me through ResNeXt, through ConvNeXt, and it's still how I try to approach research today. So in a sense, that honorable mention didn't change my plans so much as it changed my confidence that my way of doing research was okay.

r001.rationale: He says the honorable mention gave him permission to trust his own research taste and increased his confidence; he does not describe it as the beginning of his life as a researcher.
